passage:
Saturday night.
Best night in the fan group ever, at first. The other actor's fans started it after the trailer came out, and we went to war. Forty of us, memes flying, and my edit got 2k shares. Every time someone on our side wrote "legend" under it, I felt ten feet tall. We were an army. Around eleven it changed. Someone found a rival fan's profile, a girl called Neelam from Indore, and posted her school photo with a nasty caption. People piled on. Somebody mocked her looks. I typed "lol" and then didn't send it. My stomach turned. It's just a movie. She's a kid like me. I left the chat and went and showed Mummy. She didn't shout. She sat with me while we reported the post and the account, and said leaving was the right call. I can still see that photo.
Yogesh

qa.q: How many shares did Yogesh's edit get?
qa.a: The edit got 2k shares.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when someone posted Neelam's school photo?
qa.a: At first caught up in the thrill, then sick and uneasy; the stomach turned and the "lol" never got sent.

qa.q: What did Yogesh do right once the banter turned cruel?
qa.a: Yogesh didn't join in, left the chat, and showed Mummy that same night, and together they reported the post and the account.

qa.q: What might the pile-on feel like for Neelam?
qa.a: It could be frightening and humiliating to see her school photo mocked by strangers over a movie.

grounding: Yogesh's diary shows the thrill of a fan war against a rival star's fans and the moment it slides from banter into cruelty.

passage: The news broke on a Tuesday: the author of Simran's favourite fantasy series had been sending cruel messages to young writers for years, and three of them had shared screenshots. By lunch her class at the Lucknow school had split. Kritika said, "Cancel him, burn the books." Farhan said, "It's fake, it must be." Simran said nothing. At home she took the seven books off her shelf and sat on the floor with them. Those stories had got her through Class 7. Her older sister Preeti knocked. "You okay?" "I don't know what to do with them." "You don't have to decide tonight." Simran thought for a long while. "The books helped me. What he did hurt real people. Both are true." She put the books in a box, not the bin, and wrote the three writers' names in her notebook to look up their work.

qa.q: How many books did Simran take off her shelf?
qa.a: She took the seven books off her shelf.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling as she sat on the floor with the books?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and torn, because the stories had helped her but the author had hurt real people.

qa.q: Which of Simran's choices was balanced, and why?
qa.a: Boxing the books instead of binning or defending them, and looking up the three writers, kept what helped her without excusing the behaviour.

qa.q: Why might Kritika and Farhan have reacted so differently?
qa.a: Kritika's anger and Farhan's denial may both come from the same shock at a trusted author, handled in opposite ways.

grounding: Shows a teenager working through disappointment in an admired author, keeping what was good in the work without excusing the behaviour.

passage:
Jahnavi,
I'm writing because you walked out of the room last night and I couldn't say it properly.
You called Rehan Sethi arrogant because he walked out of that interview. You don't know him the way I do. I've watched every live, every backstage clip. When he says "my people", I feel he means me. I've defended him in a hundred comment threads. When people criticise him, it feels like they're criticising me, my taste, the four years I've spent loving his music.
I know he doesn't know I exist. I do know that. But last winter, alone in the PG, his voice notes to fans were the only warm thing in my day.
So maybe the interview wasn't great. I still think you were unfair. Can we get chai on Saturday and not talk about him?
Gurleen

qa.q: What did Rehan Sethi do that Jahnavi criticised?
qa.a: He walked out of that interview.

qa.q: Why does criticism of Rehan Sethi feel personal to Gurleen?
qa.a: Gurleen feels so close to him after years of his music that criticism feels like an attack on Gurleen's own taste and self, which stirs hurt and defensiveness.

qa.q: What would you advise Gurleen about the argument with Jahnavi?
qa.a: Admit plainly that the interview wasn't great, as the letter nearly does, and keep the friendship separate from the singer; the chai plan is a good start.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Gurleen's defence of the singer?
qa.a: Jahnavi may feel frustrated that any criticism is taken personally, and worried about how much the singer fills Gurleen's life.

grounding: Gurleen's letter shows a young adult defending a star whatever he does, feeling close to someone who does not know they exist.

passage:
Mentor's note, end of first semester.
Yogesh, first-year B.Sc., struggled after moving from Jalgaon. In August he ate alone and missed two mentor meetings. In October I noticed him drawing in the margins during our session: characters from an old animated series. He told me, a little shyly, that he had joined an online fan art group for it. A member there, Vasudha, from another college, had started a weekly drawing challenge, and twenty-odd members post every Sunday. "Nobody hates on anything," he said. "They just ask how you did the shading." He now runs a small sketch club at college with two classmates he met through the challenge. Next step: I've told him the art society's exhibition is in March and asked him to bring his Sunday drawings.

qa.q: How many mentor meetings did Yogesh miss in August?
qa.a: He missed two mentor meetings.

qa.q: How did Yogesh seem to feel about the fan art group?
qa.a: He felt welcomed and less lonely there, a little shy but pleased that people only asked about his shading.

qa.q: What did the mentor do next to support Yogesh?
qa.a: The mentor told him about the art society's March exhibition and asked him to bring his Sunday drawings.

qa.q: What might the weekly challenge mean to Vasudha?
qa.a: For Vasudha it may be a way to build a warm, creative circle, and seeing new members like Yogesh join probably feels rewarding.

grounding: The mentor's note shows a lonely first-year student finding friends, a creative outlet and comfort in a kind fan community.

passage: I'm Swati. Last month a film critic, Varun Kulkarni, gave our favourite actor's new film two stars. I'm a fan too, so I was annoyed, and I opened the comments ready to add mine. What I found scared me. Thousands of replies. People posting the area where he lives. Someone had found his wife's profile and was tagging her with insults. Our own fan club group, the one where I share wallpapers, was organising it: "Everyone hit the review at 8 p.m." A friend from the club messaged me, "You in?" It would have been easy. One reply, one more voice in the crowd; nobody would know it was me. I thought of his wife reading it at breakfast. I typed, "No, this isn't what being a fan means," left the group, and reported the posts sharing where he lives.

qa.q: How many stars did Varun Kulkarni give the film?
qa.a: He gave it two stars.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when the friend asked "You in?"
qa.a: Swati was tempted, since joining felt easy and anonymous, but also uneasy and scared by the cruelty.

qa.q: Which steps did Swati take, and why did they help?
qa.a: Swati refused, left the group and reported the posts sharing where he lives, which took one voice out of the crowd and helped protect the critic's family.

qa.q: What is it like for Varun's wife to be tagged by strangers?
qa.a: It is likely frightening and hurtful to be targeted over a film review she didn't even write.

grounding: Swati sees fans abusing a critic and his family online, recognises how group identity permits cruelty, and chooses not to join.

passage: I've watched football with Saurabh at the same café in Kolkata every Saturday for four years. He is the loudest supporter of our club in the room: scarf, drum, the lot. But I've seen what he does after a loss. Last month we lost on a penalty our own striker had clearly dived for. Our table erupted about the referee. Saurabh sat quietly, then said, "He dived. We'd be furious if their man did that." Nobody liked hearing it. Across the room Uday, a rival fan, was being heckled by our lot. Saurabh walked over, shook his hand and bought him a lime soda. "Good game. You deserved it." Then he came back, picked up the drum, and started the song for next week.

qa.q: Where does the narrator watch football with Saurabh?
qa.a: At the same café in Kolkata, every Saturday.

qa.q: What does Saurabh's quiet moment after the loss suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was disappointed but honest, uncomfortable letting loyalty hide that his own team's striker dived.

qa.q: How did Saurabh show loyalty and honesty together?
qa.a: He admitted the dive, treated Uday with respect, then still picked up the drum to back his club for next week.

qa.q: How might Uday have felt when Saurabh came over?
qa.a: After being heckled, Uday probably felt relieved and respected to get a handshake and a lime soda from a rival fan.

grounding: The narrator watches a devoted fan admit his team's fault and treat a rival fan kindly, showing loyalty and honesty together.

subtype: Helping together at school or in a colony [Actor]
passage:
Sunday
Dear Diary,
Today Jyoti, Pintu, six others and I cleaned the colony park! It was Jyoti's idea, because the slide was full of chips packets. Mrs Kapoor from B-block gave us gloves and big bags. I found a broken doll, forty-three wrappers (I counted) and one slipper. Pintu found a marble and said it was treasure. We filled eleven bags. My arms hurt. After lunch the little kids came, and the slide was shiny and nobody had to step over rubbish. Uncle from the ironing stall said, "Shabash, children." We're only nine kids, but the whole park looks new. Jyoti says next month the drain corner. I'm in.
Lakshmi 😊

qa.q: How many bags did the children fill?
qa.a: They filled eleven bags.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel after the clean-up?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt proud and happy, arms aching, seeing the whole park look new 😊

qa.q: What helped the clean-up work?
qa.a: Jyoti had a clear idea, Mrs Kapoor gave gloves and bags, and nine children shared the work.

qa.q: What might the clean park mean for the little kids?
qa.a: They can play on a shiny slide without stepping over rubbish, which makes the park feel like theirs again.

grounding: Lakshmi's diary shows a child joining friends in a colony clean-up and feeling proud that together they made a difference.

subtype: First cause a teenager cares about [Actor]
passage: Dhruv, you're sixteen and on fire about the lake? Good. Let your Ojas Mama tell you about my lake. At fifteen, in Bhopal, I joined a group of students trying to stop the lake edge being filled for a car park. Oh, the feeling! Banners, meetings in someone's garage, songs we wrote ourselves. For the first time I belonged to something bigger than my marks. And I was so sure. Anyone who disagreed was a villain. When our neighbour Mr Qureshi said the car park would help his little shop, I called him greedy to his face. He just looked at me, tired. Years later I learnt that shop was all that fed his family. We did save half the lake, you know. I'm still proud of that. But I wish I'd asked him one question before I judged him.

qa.q: What was the lake edge going to be filled for?
qa.a: For a car park.

qa.q: How did young Ojas feel about the campaign?
qa.a: He felt passionate and proud, belonging to something bigger than his marks, and completely sure he was right.

qa.q: What choice in the story does Ojas regret, and what would have been better?
qa.a: Calling Mr Qureshi greedy to his face; asking one question about the shop first would have kept the cause without judging a struggling neighbour.

qa.q: How might Mr Qureshi have felt when he was called greedy?
qa.a: He probably felt tired and hurt, misjudged by a teenager who didn't know the shop fed his family.

grounding: Ojas Mama recalls his first cause as a teenager: the passion and belonging, and the certainty that everyone who disagreed was wrong.

passage:
Thursday, late.
Went to the march today. Nearly didn't. At 9 a.m. I was still in the hostel, telling myself I had a lab record due and Papa would be furious if my name came up anywhere. Then Usha texted: "We're at the gate. Your choice, no pressure." That "no pressure" did it. There were maybe three hundred of us, walking from the gate to the admin block about the library closing at six. Police stood at the corner, and my heart hammered every time one of them looked our way. Usha held one end of the banner; I held the other. When we all sang outside the admin block, my throat went tight in a good way. Nobody threw anything. We left at one, as planned. Lab record still due. Haven't told Papa yet. I will, calmly, on Sunday.
Tushar

qa.q: What was the march about?
qa.a: About the library closing at six.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Tushar have at the march?
qa.a: Tushar felt fear, heart hammering when the police looked over, and also pride and closeness when everyone sang together.

qa.q: What made Tushar's decision to join a careful one?
qa.a: Tushar weighed the lab record and family worry, joined a peaceful march with a friend, and left at the planned time.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt holding the other end of the banner?
qa.a: Usha probably felt glad and supported, since the message left the choice free and Tushar still chose to come.

grounding: Tushar's diary shows a young adult joining a peaceful protest, feeling fear, pride and solidarity while weighing studies and family.

passage:
Dear Mummy and Papa,
I'm writing because on the phone last night we all shouted and nobody heard anything.
I know why you're scared. Masi forwarded you the photo of our climate sit-in, and Papa saw my face in it. You said, "What will people say? What if the police come? What about your placement?" I hung up. I'm sorry for that.
Here is what's true. The sit-in was on campus, with permission, and our professor, Dr Amandeep Gill, was there the whole time. I'm not skipping classes. I leave the moment anything feels unsafe, and I always go with Farah and two others.
I also understand that you remember things I don't, and that your fear is love.
Can we talk on Sunday, calmly? Ask me anything. I'll answer everything.
Your Rajni

qa.q: Who forwarded the photo of the sit-in to the parents?
qa.a: Masi forwarded them the photo.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling after hanging up?
qa.a: Rajni felt sorry and regretful about hanging up, while still wanting to be understood.

qa.q: Why is Rajni's letter more likely to help than the phone call?
qa.a: It names the parents' fears, answers them with facts about safety and studies, and asks for a calm talk instead of defiance.

qa.q: What is it like for Papa when he sees Rajni's face in the photo?
qa.a: Papa likely feels frightened for Rajni's safety and future, and worried about what people will say.

grounding: Rajni's letter shows a young adult answering parents' fear about activism with calm facts about risk rather than defiance.
